Content:
A compound inequality is an inequality that consists of multiple different inequalities put together. For example, the compound inequality [MATH: x \leq 0 \hspace{.25cm} \text{ or } \hspace{.25cm} x \gt 3] states that [MATH: x] is less than or equal to [MATH: 0], or greater than [MATH: 3].

Content:
For the compound "or" inequality to be satisfied, at least one of the separate inequalities must be satisfied. To illustrate:

Content:
- [MATH: x=-1] satisfies the inequality because it satisfies [MATH: x \leq 0.]
- [MATH: x=5] satisfies the inequality because it satisfies [MATH: x > 3.]
- [MATH: x=1] does not satisfy the inequality because it does not satisfy [MATH: x \leq 0] and it also does not satisfy [MATH: x > 3.]

Content:
To graph a compound inequality involving the word "or," we graph the two separate inequalities on the same number line. In this particular case,

Content:
- the inequality [MATH: x \leq 0] consists of a closed circle at [MATH: 0] and an arrow to the left, while
- the inequality [MATH: x >3] consists of an open circle at [MATH: 3] and an arrow to the right.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A compound inequality is an inequality that consists of multiple different inequalities put together. For example, the compound inequality [MATH: x \leq 0 \hspace{.25cm} \text{ or } \hspace{.25cm} x \gt 3] states that [MATH: x] is less than or equal to [MATH: 0], or greater than [MATH: 3].

Content:
For the compound "or" inequality to be satisfied, at least one of the separate inequalities must be satisfied. To illustrate:

Content:
- [MATH: x=-1] satisfies the inequality because it satisfies [MATH: x \leq 0.]
- [MATH: x=5] satisfies the inequality because it satisfies [MATH: x > 3.]
- [MATH: x=1] does not satisfy the inequality because it does not satisfy [MATH: x \leq 0] and it also does not satisfy [MATH: x > 3.]

Content:
To graph a compound inequality involving the word "or," we graph the two separate inequalities on the same number line. In this particular case,

Content:
- the inequality [MATH: x \leq 0] consists of a closed circle at [MATH: 0] and an arrow to the left, while
- the inequality [MATH: x >3] consists of an open circle at [MATH: 3] and an arrow to the right.

To graph this compound inequality, we first graph the two inequalities separately.

[IMG: /graphics/6223dd682da51dc129335dc33ff47ef1]

Content:
Then, we keep only where they overlap.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c1ab56b5765f8e0353c18be9269c2fcb]

Content:
Note: Any compound "and" inequality will always represent a segment between two points. So, it is not always necessary to draw both inequalities and find the overlap. To speed up the process, we can just draw the endpoints with open or closed circles as appropriate, and highlight the area between the endpoints.

Item 9 — Example: Representing "And" Inequalities on Number Lines

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/b4a413ddb380921dfb9a9853bb00d41e]

What inequality corresponds to the highlighted region shown on the number line above?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The red segment contains all values between [MATH: -2] and [MATH: 0.] In addition,

- the closed circle at [MATH: -2] implies that [MATH: x] can be equal to [MATH: -2,] while
- the open circle at [MATH: 0] implies that [MATH: x] cannot be equal to [MATH: 0.]

Therefore, the highlighted region represents [MATH: -2 \leq x < 0.]
